messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

When Daniel first described the worst night with his wife, he did not begin with the blow itself but with the smell. Something had scorched on the stove while they were arguing in the kitchen, a bitter burnt odor spreading through the house as her voice sharpened and he realized she was no longer simply angry but moving toward him. He remembered the confrontation in fragments of posture and tone: her face tightened, her words clipped and forceful, then the sudden physical attack at close range. What stayed with him most vividly was how quickly an ordinary domestic scene had turned dangerous. Since then, burnt food, the smell of singed metal on a job, even the faint acrid odor from an overheated motor could pull him straight back into that kitchen. Just as potent were confrontations themselves and the sound of anger in other people’s voices, not only shouting but even calm, controlled irritation. He had come to feel that anger was never just anger; it was the beginning of something worse.

In the weeks after the assault, Daniel tried to get through work and home life by narrowing his world. As a plumber, he spent his days in other people’s basements, utility rooms, and kitchens, places where there were plenty of sharp smells—burners left on, scorched dust from old furnaces, hot pipe sealant. When a burnt smell hit him unexpectedly, he would catch himself going rigid and immediately work to push the memory away. He had become practiced at cutting off any thought that might lead back to that night, telling himself not to go there, not to picture the kitchen, not to replay what had happened. The same thing happened when a customer spoke sharply to a spouse in the next room or when a contractor argued on a site; even mild confrontation made him feel cornered inside, and he would turn his attention hard toward the task in front of him or leave as soon as he could. He also stopped going into the part of the house where the assault had happened unless he absolutely had to, taking long routes around it and finding reasons to stay elsewhere. The triggers and his efforts to shut them down had become tightly linked in his everyday life.

At night, the same pattern followed him. If the house grew quiet and there was nothing to distract him, his mind edged toward the event. Daniel discovered that staying up very late felt safer than lying in bed with those thoughts. He would sit with the television on or scroll on his phone long past the point of exhaustion, trying to keep himself occupied until he was too tired to think. On evenings when he had encountered a burnt smell at work or had been around irritable customers, he was especially determined not to sleep, because he knew that once he slowed down the memory would press in. He did not describe this as a choice so much as a necessity; in his mind, if he allowed himself to think about what had happened, he would lose control of the rest of the night.

Over the months, these habits hardened. Daniel became more careful about which service calls he accepted, hesitating around jobs in homes where kitchens were the center of the work, and he was noticeably tense when clients argued in front of him. At home, he timed his movements to avoid the site of the assault, a pattern his wife noticed even when he said nothing. He kept telling himself that not thinking about it was the only way to keep functioning, yet his life was increasingly organized around not being reminded. Even a calmly angry voice in a grocery line or the smell of something burned in a restaurant kitchen could alter the rest of his day, leaving him watchful and determined to stay mentally elsewhere.

By the time he sought help, Daniel was worn down by how much effort this took. He was sleeping only in fragments because he delayed bedtime so consistently, and work had become harder because ordinary parts of the job could suddenly feel loaded with danger. What finally pushed him into treatment was the realization that his world had become smaller and more managed than he wanted to admit. He was frightened that he was beginning to live as if that night could happen anywhere there was anger or the smell of something burning. More than anything, he wanted to be able to walk into a kitchen, hear frustration in someone’s voice, and remain in the present instead of instantly bracing for harm.
